Running something again when the first time did not work.

`Schedule` says *when* and *how many times*; `retry` and `repeat` are the
two ways to drive one. `docs/vision.md` names retry policies as a
non-negotiable, and until `Clock.sleep` existed the checked-in version was
`{ attempts: Int }` -- a counter with no clock, used by nothing.

**Named for the family rather than for `retry`.** A circuit breaker, a rate
limiter, a bulkhead and a hedged request are all the same subject and none
of them is a retry; a module called `std::retry` could not hold them and
this one can. `docs/design/effect-survey.md` §3.2.

### The two things worth knowing before reading further

**A `Schedule` is a description, not a stream of instants.** It holds no
clock, so it can be compared, printed, sent to another fiber, and written
down in a test with no runtime at all. Elsewhere this type is a closure
`(attempt, elapsed) -> Option<delay>`, which is smaller and cannot do any
of that: `sharing.md` refuses a record of closures across a fiber, and a
log line saying `Exponential { base: 100, .. }` is worth more than one
saying nothing. Khora's constraints produce the better design here rather
than a compromise.

**The schedule never sleeps; the driver does.** `next_after` answers *when*
the next attempt should start, as an offset from the moment the whole thing
began, and the driver compares that to the clock and waits only for the
difference. That is what makes a schedule pure, and it is what lets
`Union`, `Intersect` and `UpTo` be real comparisons: the sooner of two
delays is not the sooner of two instants once the sides have been running
for different lengths of time.

It also lets the two honest readings of "again later" coexist without
either being a special case. `Spaced` is a **grid** -- the third attempt
begins at `3 * millis` whatever the body cost, so a run that falls behind
does not pile up delays. `Exponential` and `Fibonacci` are **backoffs**,
measured from the failure that just happened, because "wait twice as long
as last time" is a statement about the other end rather than about the
calendar. Both are instants by the time the driver sees them.

## Types

### Schedule

```khora
derive(Eq, Show)
pub type Schedule =
  | Times(n: Int)
  | Spaced(millis: Int)
  | Exponential(base: Int, factor_pct: Int, cap: Int)
  | Fibonacci(base: Int)
  | Jittered(inner: Schedule, low_pct: Int, high_pct: Int)
  | Union(left: Schedule, right: Schedule)
  | Intersect(left: Schedule, right: Schedule)
  | AndThen(first: Schedule, then: Schedule)
  | UpTo(inner: Schedule, millis: Int);
```

When to run something again, and when to stop.

Built up from small pieces rather than offered as a list of named policies,
so that the combination somebody needs and nobody anticipated is spellable:
`AndThen(Times(3), Spaced(60000))` retries hard three times and then keeps
trying once a minute, and no library had to think of that.

The two `Int`s in `Exponential` and `Jittered` are percentages rather than
floats. A policy is a thing people read in a review and a config file, and
`factor_pct: 200` is unambiguous where `2.0` invites the question of what
it multiplies -- and `Float` in a value that derives `Eq` is a trap of its
own.

#### Times

```khora
| Times(n: Int)
```

At most `n` attempts in total, with no delay between them. `1` is "do not
retry", and is what you get from `once`.

#### Spaced

```khora
| Spaced(millis: Int)
```

Every `millis`, without end.

**Anchored to the start, so it does not drift.** The third attempt begins
at `3 * millis` from the beginning whether or not the second one ran
long, which is what a caller who wrote "every thirty seconds" meant.

#### Exponential

```khora
| Exponential(base: Int, factor_pct: Int, cap: Int)
```

Wait `base`, then `base * factor_pct / 100`, and so on, never past `cap`.

The one almost every remote call wants. `Exponential(100, 200, 30000)`
waits 100ms, then 200, then 400, then 800 … capped at thirty seconds.

**Measured from the last failure, not from the beginning** — the opposite
of `Spaced`, and the two are the two honest readings of "again later". A
grid says *when* attempts happen and a backoff says *how long to leave
the other end alone*, which is a statement about the failure rather than
about the calendar. A backoff anchored to the start would shorten every
wait by however long the failing call took, which is exactly backwards:
the call that took thirty seconds to time out is the one to be most
patient after.

#### Fibonacci

```khora
| Fibonacci(base: Int)
```

Waits of `base`, `base`, `2 * base`, `3 * base`, `5 * base` …

Grows more gently than doubling, which suits a dependency that is briefly
busy rather than actually down. Measured from the last failure, as
`Exponential` is.

#### Jittered

```khora
| Jittered(inner: Schedule, low_pct: Int, high_pct: Int)
```

`inner`, with each delay multiplied by a percentage drawn from
`[low_pct, high_pct)`.

**The one that stops a thundering herd.** A thousand clients that all
failed at the same instant and all back off by exactly 100ms retry at the
same instant, which is the outage again. The draw comes from `Random`, so
it is seedable and the row says so.

#### Union

```khora
| Union(left: Schedule, right: Schedule)
```

Runs while *either* side would: the sooner of the two next instants, and
it stops only when both have.

#### Intersect

```khora
| Intersect(left: Schedule, right: Schedule)
```

Runs while *both* sides would: the later of the two next instants, and it
stops as soon as either has.

How a bound is written. `Intersect(Exponential(..), Times(5))` is "back
off, but no more than five attempts", and it is a real interval
intersection rather than a maximum of delays because the instants are
absolute.

#### AndThen

```khora
| AndThen(first: Schedule, then: Schedule)
```

`first` until it stops, then `then` from there on.

#### UpTo

```khora
| UpTo(inner: Schedule, millis: Int)
```

`inner`, but nothing after `millis` from the very beginning.

A wall-clock budget rather than an attempt count, which is usually what a
person means by "give up after a minute".

## Methods

### Schedule

```khora
impl Schedule
```

#### once

```khora
pub fn once() -> Schedule
```

Run once, and do not retry. The identity, and what you get by not asking.

#### times

```khora
pub fn times(n: Int) -> Schedule
```

Up to `n` attempts, as fast as they can be made.

#### backoff

```khora
pub fn backoff(base: Int, cap: Int) -> Schedule
```

Doubling from `base`, capped at `cap`, with the usual jitter.

**The one to reach for**, spelled out here so that the common case is not
four constructors deep. 50%–100% of the computed delay is what most
published guidance settles on: enough spread to break up a herd, not so
much that a retry arrives before the thing it is retrying could have
recovered.

#### next_after

```khora
pub fn next_after(self, attempt: Int, elapsed: Int) -> Option<Int> with { random: Random }
```

When the attempt after `attempt` should start, as milliseconds from the
beginning, or `None` to stop.

`attempt` counts the ones already made, so the first call is with `1`.
`elapsed` is what the clock says has passed since the beginning, which
only `UpTo` looks at -- a budget is the one policy that cannot be decided
from the count alone.

**An absolute instant, not a delay.** Every combinator below depends on
it: the sooner of two delays is not the sooner of two instants once the
two sides have been running for different lengths of time, and `Spaced`
only stays drift-free because it answers `attempt * millis` rather than
`millis`.

## Functions

### retry

```khora
pub fn retry<A, E, 'ef>(schedule: Schedule, body: () -> A with 'ef raises E) -> A with { 'ef | clock: Clock, random: Random } raises E
```

Runs `body` until it succeeds or the schedule runs out.

The **last** failure is the one that comes back, because it is the one that
stopped the retrying — an earlier error is a thing that was already
recovered from, and reporting it would say the wrong thing about what
happened.

The row is where the cost is written down: this needs a clock because it
waits, and a source of randomness because a schedule may be jittered. A
caller who wanted neither reaches for `Schedule::times`, and still declares
both — which is honest, since the policy is a value and could have been a
jittered one.

### retry_while

```khora
pub fn retry_while<A, E, 'ef>(schedule: Schedule, again: (E) -> Bool, body: () -> A with 'ef raises E) -> A with { 'ef | clock: Clock, random: Random } raises E
```

`retry`, for a caller that can tell a retryable failure from a permanent one.

**A predicate rather than a `Schedule` case**, which is why `Schedule` can
stay a plain ADT: "retry while the error looks like this" is a closure over
the caller's own error type, and putting one inside the description would
make the description a record of closures. The two questions are separate
anyway — *when to try again* is a policy somebody configures, *whether this
failure is worth trying again* is knowledge about the error.

Retrying a 404 is the failure this exists to prevent, and it costs the
caller one `fn`.

### repeat

```khora
pub fn repeat<A, E, 'ef>(schedule: Schedule, body: () -> A with 'ef raises E) -> Int with { 'ef | clock: Clock, random: Random }
```

Runs `body` on the schedule until it fails or the schedule runs out, and
answers how many runs succeeded.

The other half of `retry`, and the one a poller is written with:
`repeat(Schedule::Spaced(30000), fn () => reconcile()!)` is "every thirty
seconds until something breaks". The count comes back so a caller can tell
"the schedule ended" from "it never ran".
